name: Cartalax
lead: Cartalax, also written AED or T-31, is a synthetic tripeptide made of alanine, glutamate and aspartate. It was developed in Russia, and most of the published work on it comes from Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues, who study short peptides as 'bioregulators' [1].

People interested in joint and tissue recovery use it in the hope of supporting cartilage and connective tissue, which feeds into training longevity and a more youthful look. In the laboratory, it has been tested on kidney tissue cultures, skin fibroblasts and stem cells, where it influenced proliferation and aging-related markers [2].
Published work consists of cell-culture and animal studies; human data are limited [1].

chain: Short peptide marketed as a cartilage bioregulator
Aimed at joint and connective tissue upkeep
More comfortable training and a longer-lasting physique
angle.text: Users take it hoping for healthier joints and connective tissue so they can keep training and stay youthful-looking. Lab studies also examined skin fibroblasts, which is where the skin-aging interest comes from.

paras: Cartalax is the three-amino-acid sequence alanine-glutamate-aspartate. Its molecular formula is C12H19N3O8, with a molar mass of about 333 g/mol [1]. It is sold in Russian-speaking countries and online as an anti-aging and joint-support product [1].

Laboratory work includes a 2015 study in kidney explants from young and old animals, in which the short peptide AED (T-31) stimulated proliferation markers [2]. A 2020 paper looked at AED, KED and KE in aging human mesenchymal stem cell cultures and measured genes such as IGF1, FOXO1 and TERT [2]. A 2016 paper tested peptides including AED on aging skin fibroblasts, examining proliferation, apoptosis and matrix remodeling markers [2]. A 2014 Russian-language study reported that AED and EDL raised proliferation and lowered markers p16, p21 and p53 in aging kidney cell cultures [2].

Khavinson's peptides are discussed in longevity and recovery circles as alternatives to larger peptide therapies. Marketing in some markets lists arthritis among its uses, a claim Wikipedia describes as not well supported [1].

lore.intro: In recovery and anti-aging circles Cartalax is described as a cartilage-targeted short peptide.

claims.claim: Cartalax supports cartilage and joint health
claims.believers: Proponents describe it as a bioregulator that supports cartilage tissue renewal, helping joints stay comfortable for training.
claims.experts: Published studies are in cell cultures and animals; human data are limited [1][2].

card.summary: A Russian-developed three-amino-acid peptide used in the hope of supporting cartilage and joints so people can keep training and looking youthful.
card.note: Research is limited to cell and animal studies.

quick.overview:
Cartalax is a short synthetic peptide (alanine-glutamate-aspartate) developed in Russia by Vladimir Khavinson's group. People use it hoping to support cartilage and joints.

Lab studies have looked at its effect on kidney cells, skin fibroblasts and stem cells.
quick.mechanism: In cultured cells, the peptide influenced proliferation and aging-related markers and gene expression. How this relates to joints in people has not been studied.
quick.risks: No human safety data are published. It is a research-grade peptide sold online, not an approved medicine.
